title: Russia’s Plan to Break Ukraine
gist: Former Ukrainian Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba argues Russia has shifted to a new theory of victory — mass ballistic-missile and jet-drone terror on Kyiv and western cities to wreck Ukraine's economy and morale and outlast Western support — at a moment when Kyiv needs $52 billion of external financing for 2027 with only $20 billion guaranteed. He urges the EU to use the $300 billion of frozen Russian assets, fund soldiers' pay, supply long-range strike weapons without restrictions, and co-invest in Ukraine's defense industry, warning there will be no spring cease-fire.

insights.claim: Since July 2026 Russia has sharply increased ballistic-missile use and deployed fast, long-range jet-powered drones at new scale, shifting from frontline Donbas targets to mass bombing of interior cities, especially Kyiv; roughly 100 people have died in Kyiv so far.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Kuleba
insights.so_what: Escalation into Ukraine's interior raises economic disruption risk and lowers odds of near-term de-escalation.

insights.claim: Moscow no longer aims mainly to capture cities or degrade energy infrastructure but to disrupt Ukraine's entire economy and break popular morale by making urban life intolerable, driving residents and businesses to flee and turning Ukrainians against their own government.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Kuleba
insights.so_what: Ukrainian economic activity, business relocation and fiscal revenue are now the war's primary targets — negative for Ukraine's recovery and sovereign finances.
insights.quote: Russia’s principal target, then, is not Ukraine’s territory or infrastructure. It is the will of the Ukrainian people and of their partners.

themes.theme: Ukraine's financing gap and domestic reforms

insights.claim: As of September 2026 Ukraine's government estimates it needs $52 billion in external financing for 2027, only $20 billion of which is currently guaranteed.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Kuleba
insights.so_what: A $32 billion unfunded gap is a major sovereign-credit and macro-stability risk for Ukraine.

themes.theme: Frozen Russian assets and Western funding

insights.claim: Washington has made clear it will no longer provide Kyiv financial support, while the EU has budgeted roughly $100 billion in assistance for 2026-2027 and is reluctant to commit more amid its own financial and political pressures.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Kuleba
insights.so_what: Europe now bears the bulk of Ukraine's financing burden, adding pressure on EU budgets.

insights.claim: The obvious solution is giving Ukraine the $300 billion of frozen Russian assets, mostly held at Euroclear in Belgium; obstacles include litigation risk, ECB and Brussels concerns about the euro's standing and Belgium's safe-haven reputation, and Washington's desire to keep them as leverage — Kuleba urges EU states to jointly underwrite Belgium's legal exposure.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Kuleba
insights.so_what: A decision to mobilize frozen assets would be a material event for Euroclear's legal risk and for perceptions of the euro as a reserve currency.

themes.theme: Air defense arithmetic and long-range strike

insights.claim: The U.S. produces at most 840 Patriot interceptors a year to share between itself and all partners, and its stockpile is running low, while Russia produces more than 1,200 ballistic and quasi-ballistic missiles a year plus North Korean supplies.
insights.speaker: Dmytro Kuleba
insights.so_what: Interceptor supply is structurally outmatched — supporting demand for expanded missile-defense production and cheaper interceptor alternatives.

insights.so_what: Pressure to lift long-range weapons restrictions raises escalation risk but also demand for long-range strike systems.

insights.claim: Only about 30% of Ukrainian defense companies' production capacity is currently funded; Europe should launch joint ventures on EU territory, sign long-term procurement contracts that attract private capital, and open the EU's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) financing to Ukrainian firms.
